# DzGraph

> Charts for showing and exploring data, written from scratch in TypeScript: a pure core (`@dzgraph/core`: options and data in, a scene out, every series type), a DOM layer that draws it in SVG, Canvas or WebGL2 with each feature its own export (`@dzgraph/dom`), a CSS theme (`@dzgraph/theme`), an Angular wrapper (`@dzgraph/angular`) and bridges to DzTooltip and DzGrid. Accessible, right to left, time zones designed in. No runtime dependency.

Only the names written in these pages exist; do not borrow option names from other chart libraries. A chart is made with `chart(element, options, { types, features })`: each series type (`line`, `column`…) and each feature (`zoom`, `timeAxis`…) is imported and given, or it is not there. Every series has an `id`. Days (`YYYY-MM-DD`) and instants (epoch milliseconds, or ISO text with an offset) are different things. Bad input never throws: it is reported as a `Problem` (`code`, `path`, `detail`). Every sample on the documentation site (https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/) is type-checked against the published types.

This file is the documentation site's English pages (https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/) in one piece, made by scripts/llms.mjs; do not edit it by hand.

---

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/getting-started/typescript/ -->

# TypeScript

`@dzgraph/dom` draws a chart in any page, with no framework. `@dzgraph/core` holds the option types and the series
types, and `@dzgraph/theme` the CSS. This page uses `chart()` directly; the tabs show the same chart with
[Angular](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/getting-started/angular/).

## Install

```sh
npm install @dzgraph/core @dzgraph/dom @dzgraph/theme
```

No other package is needed: DzGraph has no runtime dependency.

## A first chart

The chart takes its element's size and follows it when it changes: give the element a width (a block element has one)
and a height. Without a height it takes `aspectRatio` (16:9 by default).

```html
<div id="rain" style="block-size: 320px"></div>
```

```ts
import { column, line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart } from '@dzgraph/dom';
import '@dzgraph/theme/dzgraph.css';

const c = chart(
  document.getElementById('rain')!,
  {
    title: { text: 'Rain and sun (made up)' },
    xAxis: { scale: 'category', categories: ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May', 'Jun'] },
    series: [
      { type: 'column', id: 'rain', name: 'Rain (mm)', data: [62, 48, 51, 44, 57, 39] },
      { type: 'line', id: 'sun', name: 'Sun (h)', data: [66, 92, 141, 182, 209, 236] },
    ],
  },
  { types: [column, line] },
);
```

The legend's items are buttons: a click hides a series. Tab reaches the first point; the arrow keys move along a
series and between series; the tooltip follows. The chart's words (« No data », the points' names for screen
readers) are in the language of the element or the page (`lang`): English and French are built in.

## Series types and features

A chart draws only the series types it is given (`types`), and does only what its features allow (`features`). Each is
its own import, so a page ships only what it uses:

```ts
import { area, column, line, scatter } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart, crosshair, timeAxis, zoom } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const el = document.getElementById('sales')!;
chart(el, { series: [{ type: 'area', data: [3, 5, 4] }] }, { types: [area, column, line, scatter], features: [timeAxis, zoom, crosshair] });
```

`allTypes` and `allFeatures` give everything at once, for an app that does not count bytes. An option that needs a
feature the chart was not given is not an error: the chart draws without it and reports a `missing-module` problem
(see [Problems](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/getting-started/typescript/#problems)).

| Feature | What it adds |
|---|---|
| `timeAxis` | time scales: instants and days in a zone, round ticks |
| `zoom`, `navigatorStrip` | zoom and pan; the navigator and its range buttons |
| `crosshair`, `compare`, `measure` | a crosshair, comparison from a point, a measure between two points |
| `selection`, `aggregation`, `drilldown`, `menu` | selecting points, sums or means by period, details by click, the user's menu |
| `exporting` | SVG, PNG and CSV, download and print |
| `canvas`, `webgl` | painters for many marks: Canvas past 2 000, WebGL2 for scatters past 100 000 points |

## Updating

`update()` replaces the top-level fields it is given, series matched by their `id`; `setData()` replaces one series'
values, the cheapest way to show new numbers. What the user did — a zoom, a hidden series, a selection — is their
**view**, and new options never overwrite it.

```ts
import { line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const c = chart(document.getElementById('load')!, { series: [{ type: 'line', id: 'load', name: 'Load', data: [12, 15, 11] }] }, { types: [line] });

c.update({ title: { text: 'Load (made up)' } });
c.setData('load', [12, 15, 11, 18, 16]);
```

## Events

`on()` listens to one event and returns the function that stops listening:

```ts
import { line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const c = chart(document.getElementById('load')!, { series: [{ type: 'line', id: 'load', data: [12, 15, 11] }] }, { types: [line] });

const off = c.on('pointClick', (e) => console.log(e.point.seriesId, e.point.index));
c.on('viewChange', (e) => localStorage.setItem('view', JSON.stringify(e.view)));
off();
```

The view is plain JSON: put it in a URL or a store, and give it back with `setView()`.

## Problems

Bad input never throws. A value the chart cannot read, an option it does not know, a feature it was not given: each
becomes a `Problem` — a code, a path, a detail — in `c.problems` and the `problems` event, and the chart draws what it
can. A problem never carries your data: a chart may plot health records.

```ts
import { line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const c = chart(document.getElementById('load')!, { series: [{ type: 'line', data: [12, 15, 11] }], crosshair: true }, { types: [line] });
for (const p of c.problems) console.warn(p.code, p.path); // missing-module crosshair
```

> Call `destroy()` when the element goes: it removes the chart's listeners and observers.

## The theme

`@dzgraph/theme/dzgraph.css` gives the colours and the fonts, as CSS variables, in a cascade layer (`dzgraph.theme`)
so your own rules win; `dzgraph.unlayered.css` is the same without the layer. Light and dark follow the page's
`color-scheme`: this site's switch changes the charts too.

## Next

- [Angular](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/getting-started/angular/): the same chart as a component.
- The [guides](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/data/), task by task.

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/getting-started/angular/ -->

# Angular

`@dzgraph/angular` gives two standalone components, for Angular 19 to 22: `<dz-chart>`, the whole chart, and
`<dz-sparkline>`, a small chart in a line of text or a tile. They draw with `@dzgraph/dom`; the
[TypeScript](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/getting-started/typescript/) page says what a chart does.

## Install

```sh
npm install @dzgraph/core @dzgraph/dom @dzgraph/theme @dzgraph/angular
```

Load the theme once, in the app's styles (`angular.json`'s `styles`, or a `@import` in `styles.css`):
`@dzgraph/theme/dzgraph.css`.

## A chart

The options are a signal input: a new value updates the chart, and what the user did (a zoom, a hidden series, a
selection) stays. `types` and `features` are the series types and features the chart may use: on the tag, or once for
the whole app with `provideDzGraph({ types, features })` in `bootstrapApplication` (a binding wins). The component
imports none itself, so the app ships only those it names; `provideDzGraph({ types: allTypes, features: allFeatures })`
gives everything.

```ts
import { Component } from '@angular/core';
import { bootstrapApplication } from '@angular/platform-browser';
import { allTypes } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { allFeatures } from '@dzgraph/dom';
import { provideDzGraph } from '@dzgraph/angular';

@Component({ selector: 'app-root', template: '' })
class App {}

// Every type and every feature for every chart of the app; name fewer to ship less.
void bootstrapApplication(App, { providers: [provideDzGraph({ types: allTypes, features: allFeatures })] });
```

```ts
import { line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart, crosshair, zoom } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const c = chart(
  document.getElementById('tides')!,
  {
    title: { text: 'Tide height (made up)' },
    crosshair: true,
    xAxis: { scale: 'category', categories: ['00:00', '03:00', '06:00', '09:00', '12:00', '15:00', '18:00', '21:00'] },
    series: [{ type: 'line', id: 'tide', name: 'Height (m)', data: [1.2, 3.8, 5.1, 2.4, 0.9, 3.6, 5.3, 2.2] }],
  },
  { types: [line], features: [crosshair, zoom] },
);
c.on('pointClick', (e) => console.log('Picked point', e.point.index));
```

## Outputs

Every event of the chart is an output of the component. The point events (`pointHover`, `pointClick`, `pointFocus`)
give the `PointRef` itself, `rangeChange` the range, `modeChange` the mode and `problems` the list; the others give
the event's detail: `problems`, `pointHover`,
`pointClick`, `pointFocus`, `legendToggle`, `rangeChange`, `viewChange`, `modeChange`, `measure`, `selectionChange`,
`drill`.

## The chart's methods

`chart` gives the chart itself, for its methods (`exportPng()`, `setView()`, `print()`…). It is null until the chart is
drawn (after the first render, in the browser) and on the server.

```ts
import { Component, signal, viewChild } from '@angular/core';
import { column, type ChartOptions } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { exporting } from '@dzgraph/dom';
import { DzChart } from '@dzgraph/angular';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-report',
  imports: [DzChart],
  template: `
    <dz-chart style="block-size: 300px" [options]="options()" [types]="types" [features]="features" />
    <button type="button" (click)="save()">Save as CSV</button>
  `,
})
export class Report {
  readonly chart = viewChild.required(DzChart);
  readonly types = [column];
  readonly features = [exporting];
  readonly options = signal<ChartOptions>({ series: [{ type: 'column', id: 'jars', name: 'Jars sold', data: [14, 22, 19] }] });

  async save(): Promise<void> {
    await this.chart().chart?.download('csv');
  }
}
```

## A sparkline

```ts
import { Component, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { DzSparkline } from '@dzgraph/angular';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-visits',
  imports: [DzSparkline],
  template: `<p>Visits this week <dz-sparkline [values]="visits()" [options]="{ type: 'area', label: 'Visits' }" /></p>`,
})
export class Visits {
  readonly visits = signal<readonly number[]>([31, 44, 38, 52, 49, 61, 58]);
}
```

The sparkline sizes itself to the text around it and says its summary to screen readers (« Visits: 7 values, from 31
to 61, last 58 »).

## Server rendering

On the server nothing is drawn and nothing fails: the components draw in the browser only, once their element is in
the page.

---

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/data/ -->

# Data

A series' `data` takes four shapes. Pick the one your data already has: the chart reads each without asking you to
convert. Pies and donuts take slices, and a gauge one value (see [Series types](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/series-types/)).

## Values alone

A list of numbers: each value's x is its place in the list, or the category at that place.

```ts
import type { ChartOptions } from '@dzgraph/core';

export const options: ChartOptions = {
  xAxis: { scale: 'category', categories: ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri'] },
  series: [{ type: 'column', id: 'cups', name: 'Cups of tea', data: [4, 6, 3, 7, 5] }],
};
```

## Pairs and points

Pairs `[x, y]` give each value its own x: a number, a category's name, or a date on a [time axis](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/axes-time/#time).
Points `{ x, y }` say the same, and can carry a `key` and a `name`; the tooltip and the data table show the `name`
instead of x.

```ts
import type { ChartOptions } from '@dzgraph/core';

export const pairs: ChartOptions = {
  series: [{ type: 'scatter', id: 'plants', name: 'Plants', data: [[12, 3.1], [18, 4.4], [25, 6.0]] }],
};

export const points: ChartOptions = {
  series: [
    {
      type: 'line',
      id: 'pond',
      name: 'Pond depth (m)',
      data: [
        { x: 1, y: 1.4, key: 'p-1', name: 'First survey' },
        { x: 2, y: 1.1, key: 'p-2', name: 'Second survey' },
      ],
    },
  ],
};
```

When x values are strings and the axis has no `scale`, the axis is a category axis, its categories in the order the
data gives them. When the axis lists its `categories`, a string it does not list gets a band of its own at the end,
and the chart reports it (`invalid-data`).

## Typed columns

For big series, give columns: one array per field, all of one length. A `Float64Array` for `y` is read as it is,
without a copy, so new numbers cost almost nothing. `x` may be absent: the points are then evenly spaced.

```ts
import { line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const count = 100_000;
const x = new Float64Array(count);
const y = new Float64Array(count);
for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
  x[i] = i;
  y[i] = Math.sin(i / 500) * 10;
}
chart(document.getElementById('wave')!, { series: [{ type: 'line', id: 'wave', data: { x, y } }] }, { types: [line] });
```

The [Big data](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/big-data/) guide says how such series are drawn.

## Gaps

`null` is a gap: the line breaks, the column is absent, the table cell is empty. A point alone between two gaps is
shown as a marker, or it would not be seen. In a typed column, `NaN` is a gap.

A value that is not a number in an array you wrote (`NaN`, `Infinity`, a string where a number goes) is drawn as a
gap too, and the chart reports it once for the series: a `non-finite-value` or `invalid-data` problem, with how many
points. It never says what the value was.

## Keys

A point's `key` is its identity. Selection, [linked charts](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/exploring/) and the [DzGrid bridge](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/dzgrid/) use it
to tell which point is which, whatever its place in the data. Typed columns take keys as a `key` array.

```ts
import type { ChartOptions } from '@dzgraph/core';

export const options: ChartOptions = {
  series: [
    {
      type: 'column',
      id: 'orders',
      name: 'Orders',
      data: { x: ['North', 'South', 'East'], y: [42, 35, 28], key: ['shop-n', 'shop-s', 'shop-e'] },
    },
  ],
};
```

Two points of one series with the same key: the later one is left out of selection and links, and the chart reports
`duplicate-key`.

## The order of x

Lines and areas are drawn in the order of the data. When x goes backwards, the line is drawn as given (it may cross
itself), without the [decimation](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/big-data/) that keeps long lines quick, and the chart reports `unsorted-x` once
for the series. Sort the data when the order means nothing.

## New data

`setData()` replaces one series' values: the cheapest way to show new numbers. `update()` with new `series` replaces
them whole, matched by `id`. Either way, what the user did (a zoom, a hidden series, a selection) stays.

```ts
import { line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const c = chart(
  document.getElementById('kettle')!,
  { title: { text: 'Kettle temperature (made up)' }, series: [{ type: 'line', id: 'temp', name: 'Temperature (°C)', data: [18, 24, 37] }] },
  { types: [line] },
);

const readings = [18, 24, 37];
setInterval(() => {
  readings.push(Math.min(100, readings.at(-1)! + 9));
  c.setData('temp', readings);
}, 1000);
```

> The chart never writes to your arrays. A typed `y` is read as it is; `x` is always copied, and so is a `y` that holds
> `Infinity`.

---

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/series-types/ -->

# Series types

Each series type is its own import from `@dzgraph/core`, given to the chart in `types`: a page ships only the types it
draws. `allTypes` gives them all. A series whose type the chart was not given is left out and reported
(`unknown-series-type`).

| Type | Import | Draws |
|---|---|---|
| `'line'` | `line` | points joined in x order |
| `'area'` | `area` | a line with its surface filled down to zero |
| `'column'` | `column` | upright rectangles from zero, side by side in each category |
| `'bar'` | `bar` | columns turned across: the chart becomes horizontal |
| `'scatter'` | `scatter` | one marker per point, placed by two values |
| `'pie'`, `'donut'` | `pie`, `donut` | the parts of one whole, as slices |
| `'gauge'` | `gauge` | one value on a half ring |

## Lines and areas

Points are joined in x order by straight segments; a gap breaks the line (see [Data](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/data/#gaps)). Markers show on
every point when there is room to read them; a denser line keeps one about every 80 px. `marker: true` puts one on
every point, `false` none. Each series has its own marker symbol (circle, square, diamond, triangle…), so series are
told apart without colour.

An area is a line with its surface filled down to zero, translucent, the line on top. Areas and columns always have
zero on their axis; lines and scatters fit their data.

## Columns and bars

Columns stand side by side in each category's band, in series order. Negative values go down from a stronger zero
line. A chart with bars is horizontal: the categories run down from the top, the values grow along the reading
direction. A chart has one orientation: bars and columns together are reported (`mixed-orientation`).

## Stacks

Columns, bars or areas with the same `stack` name pile on each other (`stack: true` is the stack named `default`).
Positive values pile upwards, negative ones downwards. `stacking: 'percent'` on the y axis turns each pile into
shares of its total, from 0 to 100 %. The tooltip gives a part's value, its share and the pile's total; the data
table adds a total column.

```ts
import { column } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart } from '@dzgraph/dom';

chart(
  document.getElementById('harvest')!,
  {
    title: { text: 'Harvest by plot (made up)' },
    xAxis: { scale: 'category', categories: ['June', 'July', 'August', 'September'] },
    yAxis: { title: 'kg' },
    series: [
      { type: 'column', id: 'beans', name: 'Beans', stack: 'veg', data: [40, 85, 120, 60] },
      { type: 'column', id: 'peas', name: 'Peas', stack: 'veg', data: [70, 55, 20, 10] },
      { type: 'column', id: 'squash', name: 'Squash', stack: 'veg', data: [0, 30, 95, 140] },
    ],
  },
  { types: [column] },
);
```

Lines do not stack: a stacked line would read as its own values, which it is not. `stack` on a line is reported
(`unknown-option`); an app that wants a running total computes it.

## Mixing types

Columns, bars, lines, areas and scatters mix on one x axis, drawn in series order. A line over categories passes
through the middle of each band. Two measures of different units go on two value axes (see
[Axes and time](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/axes-time/#two-value-axes)). A pie or a gauge does not mix with them: a chart has one coordinate
system, the one of its first series.

## Scatter plots

Each point is a marker placed by its x and its y, both axes fitted to the data. Markers are slightly translucent, so
piles of points read darker. Past 2 000 markers they are painted on a Canvas, past 100 000 with WebGL2 (the `canvas`
and `webgl` features, see [Big data](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/big-data/)).

## Pies and donuts

A pie's data are slices: pairs `['Apples', 120]`, points `{ name, y, key }`, or values alone. Slices start at the top
and follow clockwise, in data order. Past seven slices, the six largest stay and the rest join one slice « Others »,
with any slice under 2 % (`others: false` stops it). A donut's hole holds the total; `hole` sets its size (0 to 0.9, default 0.6) and `center` what it says.

Labels sit outside, with a leader line and the share in %. When they do not fit, the pie shows its legend instead. One
pie or donut per chart.

## Gauges

A gauge shows one value (`data: 72`) on a half ring from `min` (0) to `max` (100). `thresholds` draw a thin ring of
ranges outside the arc; the label of the range the value falls in is written under the value, so it is not told by
colour alone.

```ts
import type { ChartOptions } from '@dzgraph/core';

export const options: ChartOptions = {
  title: { text: 'Water tank (made up)' },
  series: [
    {
      type: 'gauge',
      id: 'tank',
      name: 'Water tank (%)',
      data: 64,
      thresholds: [
        { from: 0, to: 20, label: 'Low', color: 'low' },
        { from: 20, to: 80, label: 'Fine' },
        { from: 80, to: 100, label: 'Full' },
      ],
    },
  ],
};
```

## Colours

A series takes the theme's colours in order. `color` picks another: a place in the palette (`color: 3`, counting from
1), or a colour of your own, `{ token: 'brand' }`, which you define in CSS as `--dzgraph-color-brand`. A threshold's
`color` names such a colour too. Colours are never written in the options: they live in CSS, so light and dark mode
and the contrast checks hold.

> Colour is never the only way to tell series apart: each has its marker symbol, its sign in the legend and its name in
> the tooltip and the data table.

---

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/axes-time/ -->

# Axes and time

A chart has an x axis and a y axis, guessed from the data when the options leave them out. `xAxis` and `yAxis` take
one axis, or a list of them. An axis's `scale` says how it turns values into positions.

| `scale` | Values | When |
|---|---|---|
| `'linear'` | numbers | the default for numbers |
| `'category'` | names, one band each | the default when x values are strings |
| `'log'` | positive numbers, each power of ten the same length | values over several orders of magnitude |
| `'time'` | instants and calendar days, in a zone | with the `timeAxis` feature |

## Bounds and ticks

A value axis fits the data and rounds its ends outwards to ticks: values from 13 to 87 give an axis from 0 to 100.
Columns, bars and areas always have zero on their axis; lines and scatters do not force it in. `min` and `max` are
kept exactly as given. Ticks fall on round steps (1, 2, 2.5 or 5 times a power of ten), about one every 64 px upright;
`ticks.target` asks for another count. Labels follow the chart's locale, and large numbers shorten (`12K`, `3.4M`).

```ts
import type { ChartOptions } from '@dzgraph/core';

export const options: ChartOptions = {
  yAxis: {
    scale: 'linear',
    title: 'Weight',
    min: 0,
    ticks: { target: 4, format: (v, context) => `${v.toLocaleString(context.locale)} kg` },
  },
  series: [{ type: 'line', id: 'pumpkin', name: 'Pumpkin', data: [2.5, 4.1, 6.8, 9.2] }],
};
```

`ticks.grid` turns gridlines on or off (on for value axes, off for the x axis). `reversed` runs an axis from its end
to its start. `opposite` puts it on the far side: an x axis at the top, a y axis at the end of the reading direction.
`title` writes the axis's name beyond its labels.

A category axis has one band per category, its label centred under the band. Labels that would overlap are turned by
45°, then every second (third…) one is shown, always the first.

## Logarithmic scale

`scale: 'log'` on a value axis: base ten, each power of ten the same length. A value of zero or below has no place on
it: the point becomes a gap and the series reports `non-positive-log-value` once, with how many points. It is never
moved to a small number to be drawn.

Stacking on a log axis is reported (`invalid-option`): a pile's parts do not add up along it.

## Time

`scale: 'time'` needs the `timeAxis` feature (without it the axis is drawn linear and the chart reports
`missing-module`). It reads three kinds of x:

- **instants** as numbers: milliseconds since 1970 UTC;
- **instants** as ISO strings with an offset: `2026-03-29T01:30:00+01:00`, `2026-03-29T00:30:00Z`;
- **calendar days**: `2026-03-29`, placed at that day's midnight in the axis's zone.

A date-time without an offset (`2026-03-29T01:30`) is never guessed: the point is a gap, and the chart reports
`ambiguous-instant`. Ticks fall on round wall-clock values (years, months, days, hours…). A label says only what
changes at its unit (« 2026 », « Mar », « 3 », « 14:00 »), and when ticks are days or finer, a second row names the
month or the date.

```ts
import { column } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart, timeAxis } from '@dzgraph/dom';

chart(
  document.getElementById('eggs')!,
  {
    title: { text: 'Eggs laid (made up)' },
    xAxis: { scale: 'time', zone: 'Europe/Paris' },
    series: [
      {
        type: 'column',
        id: 'eggs',
        name: 'Eggs',
        data: [['2026-03-27', 5], ['2026-03-28', 7], ['2026-03-29', 6], ['2026-03-30', 8], ['2026-03-31', 4]],
      },
    ],
  },
  { types: [column], features: [timeAxis] },
);
```

Three days of readings, one a minute: drag across the plot to zoom down to hours and minutes, and the ticks follow.

## Time zones

An axis reads instants in its `zone`, an IANA name (`'Europe/Paris'`, `'America/Los_Angeles'`); without one, the
page's zone. Ticks, labels, the tooltip and the data table all read that zone's wall clock. A day tick stands at local
midnight even on a day of 23 or 25 hours; an hour the clock repeats has two ticks, an hour it skips has none.

```ts
import type { ChartOptions } from '@dzgraph/core';

export const options: ChartOptions = {
  xAxis: { scale: 'time', zone: 'Pacific/Auckland', min: '2026-04-04T00:00:00+13:00', max: '2026-04-06T00:00:00+12:00' },
  series: [{ type: 'line', id: 'tide', name: 'Tide (m)', data: [[Date.UTC(2026, 3, 4, 3), 1.2], [Date.UTC(2026, 3, 4, 9), 2.6]] }],
};
```

> Days and instants are different things. A calendar day has no zone; an instant has no calendar until a zone reads it.
> DzGraph never turns one into the other without the axis's zone, so a chart reads the same on every machine.

## Two value axes

Two measures of different units each get their own value axis: give `yAxis` a list, the second `opposite`, and name
it on its series (`yAxis: 'y2'`; axes are `y`, `y2`, `y3`… unless you give them an `id`). The second axis's ticks fall
on the first one's gridlines, so one set of gridlines serves both. Each axis shows the signs of its series before its
title, so the reader knows which series is read where without relying on colour.

---

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/interactions/ -->

# Interactions

Everything on this page comes with `chart()` itself: no feature to import. Zooming, the crosshair, selecting and the
other ways to explore are in [Exploring](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/exploring/).

## The tooltip

Over lines and areas the tooltip is **shared**: the x nearest the pointer is found, anywhere up or down the plot, and
every visible line gives its value there. Over columns, bars and scatters it is **per mark**: the column in whose band
the pointer is, or the scatter point within 24 px. A chart mixing both gives the mark its own tooltip and the lines
their shared one elsewhere.

The tooltip names the point (its category, its x or its name), then gives one row per series: its sign, as in the
legend, its name and its value in the chart's language. It sits on the end side of the reading direction, never over
the point, and goes when the pointer leaves the plot. On a touch screen a tap shows it and a slide moves it.

While a column, a bar or a scatter point is pointed at, the other series fade to 35 %: the **highlight**.
`highlight: false` turns it off. A shared line tooltip fades nothing, since every line is in it.

The tooltip is for the eyes only. Keyboard and screen-reader users get the same content from the focused point (see
[The keyboard](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/interactions/#the-keyboard)). To draw it with DzTooltip, see [DzTooltip](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/dztooltip/).

## Pointing from the app

`pointHover` says which point the pointer is on (`null` when it leaves), `pointClick` which one was clicked or
tapped. `showX()` does the reverse: it shows the tooltip and the crosshair at an x value, as if the user pointed
there, without sending `pointHover` back.

```ts
import { line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const c = chart(document.getElementById('visits')!, { series: [{ type: 'line', id: 'visits', data: [31, 44, 38, 52] }] }, { types: [line] });

c.on('pointHover', (e) => console.log(e.point ? e.point.index : 'left the plot'));
c.showX(2);
c.showX(null);
```

## The legend

The legend shows when there are two series or more. Each item is a toggle button: a click, or Enter or Space on a
focused item, hides its series, and the axes are worked out again without it. Pointing at an item fades the other
series. Hiding every series is allowed: the plot then says there is no data.

A hidden series is part of what the user did (their [view](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/exploring/#the-view-as-json)), not an option:
`initiallyHidden` hides a series only the first time it appears, so options rebuilt later never show it again by
surprise. `setSeriesVisible()` hides or shows one from the app; `legendToggle` says when the user did.

```ts
import { line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const c = chart(
  document.getElementById('beds')!,
  {
    title: { text: 'Garden beds watered (made up)' },
    legend: { position: 'end', align: 'start' },
    series: [
      { type: 'line', id: 'roses', name: 'Roses', data: [3, 4, 2, 5] },
      { type: 'line', id: 'herbs', name: 'Herbs', data: [6, 5, 7, 6] },
      { type: 'line', id: 'beans', name: 'Beans', data: [1, 2, 2, 4], initiallyHidden: true },
    ],
  },
  { types: [line] },
);
c.on('legendToggle', (e) => console.log(e.seriesId, e.shown ? 'shown' : 'hidden'));
c.setSeriesVisible('beans', true);
```

`legend: false` hides the legend. `position` puts it at the `top`, the `bottom` (the default), the `start` or the
`end` of the reading direction; `align` places it along that side.

## The keyboard

The chart's points are one tab stop; the legend's items come after them. Every point can be reached, even those a
dense line does not draw: the focus ring shows where the point is, and the tooltip and the crosshair follow.

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| Tab | to the point focused last (the first point the first time), then the legend, then out |
| ← → | the previous or next point along x, as drawn (in bars: between series) |
| ↑ ↓ | the series above or below at the same x (in bars: along the categories) |
| Home, End | the series' first or last point |
| Page Up, Page Down | a tenth of the series' points back or forward |
| Enter | a click on the point (`pointClick`) |
| Escape | hides the tooltip; the focus stays |

Focus changes send `pointFocus`. The zoom, selection, measure and drill keys are in [Exploring](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/exploring/).

## Animation

A chart appears in 400 ms: lines are revealed from the start of the x axis, columns grow from their baseline, points
fade in. An update moves what stays to where it goes in 250 ms; a legend click animates the same way; a resize does
not. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, or with `animation: false`, the end state is drawn at once.

An app may drive the animation itself with the `animate` hook (GSAP, for one): it receives both states, the duration
the chart would take, and a function that draws any state between them.

```ts
import { line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart } from '@dzgraph/dom';

chart(document.getElementById('slow')!, { series: [{ type: 'line', data: [3, 5, 4, 6] }] }, {
  types: [line],
  animate: (a) => {
    const start = performance.now();
    const frame = (now: number) => {
      const t = Math.min(1, (now - start) / (a.duration * 3));
      a.draw(1 - (1 - t) ** 3);
      if (t < 1) requestAnimationFrame(frame);
      else a.done();
    };
    requestAnimationFrame(frame);
  },
});
```

## The chart's words

The words the chart says or shows (« No data », the points' names for screen readers, the buttons' names) follow
the language of the element or the page; English and French are built in. `messages` changes some or all of them;
with Angular, the `messages` input does the same.

```ts
import { line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart } from '@dzgraph/dom';

chart(document.getElementById('empty')!, { series: [{ type: 'line', data: [] }] }, { types: [line], messages: { noData: 'Nothing measured yet' } });
```

---

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/exploring/ -->

# Exploring

Each way to explore is a feature of `@dzgraph/dom`, imported on its own and given to `chart()` in `features`
(see [Series types and features](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/getting-started/typescript/#series-types-and-features)). What the user finds
while exploring — a range, a selection, a comparison — is their **view**: plain JSON the app can keep and give back.

## Zoom and pan

With the `zoom` feature, a drag across the plot zooms to the x range it covers; Shift + drag moves the range once
zoomed; Ctrl (⌘ on a Mac) + wheel zooms around the pointer, and a plain wheel still scrolls the page. On a touch
screen, a pinch zooms and a one-finger slide moves the range. Value axes fit the points in view, and a « Reset zoom »
button goes back to the whole. The chart never zooms past the data's ends.

`rangeChange` gives the visible bounds (`null` for the whole); `setRange()` sets them from the app, with numbers or,
on a time axis, ISO dates.

## The navigator and range buttons

`navigator: true`, with the `navigatorStrip` feature (it brings `zoom`), draws a strip under the plot with the
whole x range and a window over the visible part. Drag the window to move the range, a handle to move one end; both
handles are sliders for the keyboard. On a time axis, buttons above the plot (« 1m », « 3m », « YTD », « 1y »,
« All ») show the last month, the last three months, the year so far, the last year or everything
(`rangeButtons: false` hides them); a button longer than the data is disabled.

`crosshair: true`, with the `crosshair` feature, adds lines through the pointer and its values on the axes
(`{ horizontal: true }` for the horizontal line too).

```ts
import { line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart, crosshair, navigatorStrip, timeAxis } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const c = chart(
  document.getElementById('sensor')!,
  { navigator: true, crosshair: true, xAxis: { scale: 'time', zone: 'UTC' }, series: [{ type: 'line', id: 'sensor', data: [['2026-01-01T00:00:00Z', 100], ['2026-01-01T00:01:00Z', 101]] }] },
  { types: [line], features: [timeAxis, navigatorStrip, crosshair] },
);
c.on('rangeChange', (e) => console.log(e.range));
c.setRange({ min: '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z', max: '2026-01-01T00:01:00Z' });
```

## Modes: zoom, select, measure

A drag across the plot does one thing at a time. With two or more of the `zoom`, `selection` and `measure` features,
a row of buttons at the start of the plot's top edge chooses which: « Zoom », « Select », « Measure ».
`setMode()` chooses from the app, and `modeChange` says when the user did. A chart with `selection` alone selects on
drag.

## Measure

In measure mode, press on a point and drag to another: a line joins them and a tag gives the difference in value,
in percent and along x (a duration on a time axis). The two points may be of different series. Escape, a click
elsewhere or new data removes it; zooming keeps it on its points. With the keyboard, M on a focused point starts a
measure, the arrows move its end, M keeps it. `measure` gives the two points, `null` when it goes.

## Selection

`selection: true`, with the `selection` feature, lets the user select points: a range of x on lines and areas, a
rectangle on scatters, columns and bars; `shapes` lists those offered (`rectangle`, `range`, `lasso`). The lasso is
exact, even on a million points. Shift adds, Alt removes; a click selects one point, Shift + click adds it; Escape or
a click on empty plot clears. With the keyboard, Space selects the focused point. Selected points keep their colour
and the others fade.

The selection is data, not pixels: it lasts through zoom, resize and hidden series. `selectionChange` gives the
indices, the keys and the x values per series; `selectBy()` selects from the app by key or by x.

```ts
import { scatter } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart, selection } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const c = chart(
  document.getElementById('trees')!,
  { selection: true, series: [{ type: 'scatter', id: 'trees', data: [{ x: 2, y: 3, key: 'oak' }, { x: 4, y: 1, key: 'elm' }, { x: 5, y: 4, key: 'yew' }] }] },
  { types: [scatter], features: [selection] },
);
c.on('selectionChange', (e) => console.log(e.count, e.series.map((s) => s.keys)));
c.selectBy('key', ['oak', 'yew']);
```

## Comparison and the menu

`compare` on a y axis, with the `compare` feature, draws each series against its first point in view: `value` as
the difference, `percent` as the change in percent, `index` as base 100. `compareTo` fixes the baseline at an x.
Zooming moves a baseline that is not fixed. The tooltip gives the compared value, then the raw one.

The `menu` feature adds a « Chart options » button at the end of the top edge. `menu: true` offers everything that
makes sense for the data; `{ items }` chooses: a series' `type`, the `aggregation`, the `scale` (linear or
logarithmic), the comparison (`compare`), and with `exporting`, `export` and `print`. A choice is part of the view.

## Aggregation

`aggregate` on the x axis, with the `aggregation` feature, draws one point per period of a time axis (`hour`, `day`,
`week`, `month`, `quarter`, `year`, on the zone's calendar) or per bucket of a number axis (`{ step }`). Each series
says how (`aggregate`: `sum`, `mean`, `min`, `max`, `count`); columns and bars sum by default, the others take the
mean. A period without points is a gap, not a zero. The tooltip names the period and how many points it holds.

```ts
import { column } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { aggregation, chart, timeAxis } from '@dzgraph/dom';

chart(
  document.getElementById('rain')!,
  {
    xAxis: { scale: 'time', zone: 'Europe/Paris', aggregate: 'month' },
    series: [{ type: 'column', id: 'rain', name: 'Rain (mm)', aggregate: 'sum', data: [['2026-01-05', 12], ['2026-01-19', 4], ['2026-02-02', 9]] }],
  },
  { types: [column], features: [timeAxis, aggregation] },
);
```

## Drilldown

A click or Enter on a point that has a detail shows the detail in its place; a breadcrumb above the plot goes back,
as do Backspace and Alt + ←. Going back restores the level as it was. `drill` gives the path of keys.

`drilldown: 'time'`, with the `drilldown` feature (it brings `aggregation`), starts a time axis at years and drills
a year into its months, a month into its days. Click a year, then a month:

A series' `drilldown` gives each point's detail by the point's key (`details`), or loads it (`load`, a function
returning a promise of series); a load that fails or takes more than 10 s says so and offers to retry. Click a fruit:

## The keys for exploring

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| + − | zoom in or out around the focused point |
| Shift + ← → | move the visible range (in selection mode: extend the selection) |
| 0 | back to the whole |
| Space | select or unselect the focused point |
| M | start a measure on the focused point, then keep it |
| Enter | a point's detail |
| Backspace, Alt + ← | up one level of detail |
| Escape | remove the measure, clear the selection |

## The view as JSON

The view holds what the user changed while exploring, and only that: hidden series, the visible range, the
comparison, the selection, the aggregation, the drill level, a series' type, the scale. It names series by id and
points by key (or index), never by their values. `getView()` gives it, `setView()` gives it back, `viewChange` says
what changed and who changed it. What it names that no longer exists is left out and reported (`invalid-view`).
The mode and a measure are not part of it: they are how the user works, not what they found.

```ts
import { line, type ChartView } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart, zoom } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const c = chart(document.getElementById('load')!, { series: [{ type: 'line', id: 'load', data: [12, 15, 11, 18, 16] }] }, { types: [line], features: [zoom] });

const saved = localStorage.getItem('load-view');
if (saved) c.setView(JSON.parse(saved) as ChartView);
c.on('viewChange', (e) => {
  if (e.source === 'user') localStorage.setItem('load-view', JSON.stringify(e.view));
});
```

## Linked charts

`linkCharts()` makes charts follow each other, by value and never by pixel: the crosshair and the tooltip at the
same x, the same visible range, the same selected points (by key or by x), the same drill level. It returns the
function that unlinks them; a chart destroyed leaves its groups by itself.

```ts
import { column, line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart, crosshair, linkCharts, selection, zoom, type ChartSetup } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const setup: ChartSetup = { types: [line, column], features: [zoom, crosshair, selection] };
const price = chart(document.getElementById('price')!, { crosshair: true, series: [{ type: 'line', data: [10, 12, 11, 14] }] }, setup);
const volume = chart(document.getElementById('volume')!, { crosshair: true, series: [{ type: 'column', data: [300, 420, 380, 510] }] }, setup);

const unlink = linkCharts([price, volume], { crosshair: true, zoom: 'x', selection: 'x' });
unlink();
```

---

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/big-data/ -->

# Big data

DzGraph draws lines of ten million points and scatters of millions and keeps zooming and panning them fluid. Nothing
needs turning on for lines; marks in great numbers want the `canvas` feature, and dense scatters the `webgl` one.
The pictures are the same whichever way they are painted.

## Data in columns

The fastest data is a pair of columns: `{ x, y }` as `Float64Array`s (`x` optional, `key` an optional array of
strings). The chart reads them without a copy. On a time axis, `x` holds instants in milliseconds since 1970 (UTC).

To show new numbers, write into the columns and give them again with `setData()`: the chart reads them again, and
forgets what it had worked out from their old values.

```ts
import { line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart, timeAxis } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const n = 1_000_000;
const x = new Float64Array(n);
const y = new Float64Array(n);
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  x[i] = Date.UTC(2026, 0, 1) + i * 60_000;
  y[i] = Math.sin(i / 5000) * 10 + 50;
}

const c = chart(document.getElementById('flow')!, { xAxis: { scale: 'time' }, series: [{ type: 'line', id: 'flow', name: 'Flow (made up)', data: { x, y } }] }, { types: [line], features: [timeAxis] });

y[n - 1] = 75;
c.setData('flow', { x, y });
```

A gap is `NaN` in a column (`null` in an array). On a line or an area, x going backwards is reported
(`unsorted-x`); a scatter's x may come in any order.

## Lines: decimation

A line with more points than the plot has pixel columns is drawn from far fewer points: for each pixel column, the
first, the last, the lowest and the highest (M4). It looks the same to the eye, every peak kept, and a frame costs
about the same whatever the length. The tooltip, the keyboard and the data table always give the real points. Zoom
into this line of a million made-up points: the detail appears as you go.

The data table for screen readers lists at most 1 000 rows (those of the visible range when zoomed) and says how many
it leaves out.

## Many marks: Canvas

With the `canvas` feature, a series drawing more than 2 000 marks (markers, columns, scatter points) is painted on a
Canvas under the axes and labels, with the same colours and sizes, aligned to the pixel. Without it every series is
drawn in SVG: the same picture, slower past a few thousand elements. Hovering finds the nearest point at once, however
many there are.

## Dense scatters: WebGL2

With the `webgl` feature (it brings `canvas`), a scatter of more than 100 000 points is drawn by WebGL2. The points
stay on the graphics card: a zoom or a pan moves the view, not the points, and costs almost no script. Colours,
symbols, sizes and translucency are those of the Canvas picture, so piles read darker the same way. Lasso a part of
this cloud of 200 000 made-up points, or zoom into it:

> A page has only about sixteen WebGL contexts. A chart opens one only when it first draws a dense scatter, and frees it
> when destroyed. Without WebGL2 (an old browser, too many contexts, the graphics card lost) the same picture is drawn on
> Canvas, and WebGL2 takes over again when it can.

## What the benches measured

The thresholds come from measures, not guesses: Canvas draws 100 000 points in about 3 ms of script a frame, and its
cost grows with each point, where WebGL2's does not. The benches run in real Chrome; the figures below are medians in
milliseconds of script (2026-11-23), against 16.7 ms for 60 frames a second. They are in
[bench/results](https://github.com/plinthworks/dzgraph/tree/main/bench/results); `npm run bench` measures again on
your machine.

| Chart | First drawing | A zoom frame | A pan frame |
|---|---|---|---|
| line, 10 million points | 328 | 2.7 | 2.3 |
| time axis, 1 million points, navigator | 70 | 5.4 | 5.3 |
| scatter, 100 000 points (Canvas) | 24 | 3.4 | 2.1 |
| scatter, 1 million points (WebGL2) | 89 | 0.7 | 2.2 |
| scatter, 10 million points (WebGL2) | 497 | 1.0 | 1.9 |

The lasso stays live too: on a million points, each move of the pointer costs about 5 ms.

---

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/exporting/ -->

# Export and print

The `exporting` feature turns a chart into a file: a picture (SVG, PNG), its numbers (CSV), or a printed page. Everything
is made in the page; nothing is sent to a server. Without the feature, the export methods do nothing and report a
`missing-module` problem.

## What a picture shows

A picture is the **view**, as on screen: the visible range, without the hidden series, with the selection, the
comparison, the aggregation and the drill level, and with the title, the axes and the legend. The tools are left out:
no mode bar, menu button, zoom reset button, breadcrumb, navigator or range buttons, and no tooltip, crosshair or
focus ring. A picture shows the data, not the tools.

- **Colours** are those of the screen (a dark page exports dark), unless the picture asks for `theme: 'light'` or
  `'dark'`. The background is always painted, never transparent.
- **Size**: the chart's size on screen. `width` and `height` lay the chart out again at that size (labels, ticks and
  legend fit it); they do not stretch the picture.
- **SVG** is a standalone document: colours and fonts are written as values, so it needs no theme. It has
  `role="img"`, a `<title>` (the chart's title) and a `<desc>` (the summary screen readers hear), the language and the
  direction. A dense scatter gives one element per point: use PNG for it.
- **PNG** is drawn at `scale` device pixels per CSS pixel (by default the screen's, at least 2). Marks the screen
  paints with Canvas or WebGL2 are in it too.
- **The file name** comes from the title (letters, digits and hyphens), else « chart »; `exporting.filename` sets it.

## From the code

```ts
import { column } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart, exporting } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const c = chart(
  document.getElementById('harvest')!,
  {
    title: { text: 'Crates picked (made up)' },
    xAxis: { scale: 'category', categories: ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri'] },
    series: [{ type: 'column', id: 'crates', name: 'Crates', data: [12, 19, 15, 22, 17] }],
    exporting: { filename: 'crates' },
  },
  { types: [column], features: [exporting] },
);

document.getElementById('save')!.addEventListener('click', () => void c.download('png'));

const svg = c.exportSvg({ theme: 'light' }); // a standalone SVG document
const png = await c.exportPng({ width: 1200, height: 630, scale: 2 }); // a Blob, for a link preview
const csv = c.exportCsv(); // the numbers, as text
```

`exportSvg()` and `exportCsv()` give text (null without the feature); `exportPng()` gives a `Blob`; `download()`
saves a file in the format named (`'png'`, `'svg'` or `'csv'`).

## The user's menu

With the `menu` feature, `menu: true` puts a small button at the top of the chart; its « Download » item opens PNG, SVG
and CSV, and « Print » prints. `menu: { items: ['export', 'print'] }` offers only those two. Try it on this chart:

## The numbers as CSV

The CSV has the same columns as the [data table](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/accessibility/#the-data-table): the x values, then one column
per visible series. It has the rows the table shows (the visible range, or all the data when the table was switched to
it), but every one of them, with no limit.

- Values are raw: `1234.5`, never « 1 234,5 € »; an empty cell for a gap.
- Times are ISO 8601 with their offset, in the axis's zone (`2026-03-08T02:00:00+01:00`); days alone (`2026-03-08`)
  when every time is a midnight.
- By default it is universal: commas between cells, a dot for decimals, UTF-8 with a byte order mark so a spreadsheet
  reads accents. `exporting: { csv: { locale: true } }` (or `exportCsv({ locale: true })`) writes semicolons and a
  decimal comma when the chart's language writes decimals with a comma, which a French spreadsheet opens as columns.
- A text cell that starts like a formula (`=`, `+`, `-`, `@`) is written after an apostrophe, so a spreadsheet does not
  run it. Numbers are never touched.

## Printing

`print()` prints the chart alone on a page: the picture above, in light colours (paper is light), fitted to the page's
width. `print({ table: true })` adds the data table under it. It prints from a hidden frame: the page around the
chart does not move, and the chart on screen keeps its view and its focus.

A page printed whole, with the browser's Print, prints each chart in light colours too, without its tools, and never
cut between two sheets. That part is the theme's work: it holds even without the `exporting` feature.

> Nothing leaves the browser: the export never calls a remote service, so a chart of private numbers stays private.

---

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/accessibility/ -->

# Accessibility

A chart is for everyone who reads the page: with a mouse, with a keyboard, with a screen reader, without telling
colours apart, or on paper. None of this is an option to turn on: every chart does it.

Press Tab to reach the chart's points, then the arrow keys; the data table under the chart is the one screen readers
read.

## The keyboard

The chart's points are one tab stop: Tab lands on the point focused last (the first time, the first point of the first
visible series). Tab again goes on to the legend's items, then out of the chart.

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| ← → | the previous or next point along x, as drawn (a mirrored axis turns them with it) |
| ↑ ↓ | the series above or below, at the same x; in bars, along the categories |
| Home, End | the series' first and last point |
| Page Up, Page Down | a tenth of the series' points |
| Enter | a click on the point (`pointClick`) |
| Escape | hides the tooltip; the focus stays |
| `+` `-` `0` | with `zoom`: zoom in and out around the point, back to the whole |

The focused point has a visible ring (`--dzgraph-focus`), and the crosshair and tooltip of a hover. Every point can be
reached, also those a dense line draws without a marker: the ring shows where it is. The legend's items are toggle
buttons: Enter or Space hides or shows a series.

## Screen readers

The chart is a figure named by its title, described by a summary written for it: its kind, its series and the range
of each, then the app's `description` when it gives one. Each visible series is a list (« Plum, 6 points »), each
point an item read as « Plum, Aug: 66. Point 4 of 6. ». A series of more than 500 points is not written out: one item
stands for the focused point and changes as the focus moves.

Axes, gridlines, tick labels and the legend's signs are hidden from screen readers: what they say is in the summary,
the points and the data table. A polite live region says what the user changed (« Quince hidden »); data updates are
not announced. The words are English or French, after the page's language; others can be given (see
[the chart's words](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/theming-rtl/#the-charts-words)).

```ts
import { line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart } from '@dzgraph/dom';

chart(
  document.getElementById('jam')!,
  {
    title: { text: 'Jars of jam sold (made up)' },
    description: 'Plum jam sells best in late summer.',
    dataTable: true,
    xAxis: { scale: 'category', categories: ['May', 'Jun', 'Jul', 'Aug', 'Sep', 'Oct'] },
    series: [
      { type: 'line', id: 'plum', name: 'Plum', data: [14, 22, 41, 66, 58, 30] },
      { type: 'line', id: 'quince', name: 'Quince', data: [8, 9, 12, 18, 35, 52] },
    ],
  },
  { types: [line] },
);
```

## The data table

Every chart has a table with the same numbers: a caption (the title), a first column of x values, then one column per
visible series, values written as in the tooltip. It is hidden from sight but read by screen readers, after the chart;
`dataTable: true` shows it under the chart.

- It has at most 1 000 rows; past that, its last row says how many were left out (the [CSV
  export](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/exporting/#the-numbers-as-csv) gives them all).
- Zoomed, it shows the visible range and says so in its caption; a button under it switches to all the data and back.
  `dataTable: { show: true, rows: 'all' }` starts with all the data.

## Never colour alone

Colour is never the only way to tell series apart:

- Each series has its own marker symbol: circle, square, diamond, triangle, triangle pointing down, then again. A line
  shows markers on every point when they are far enough apart, and about every 80 px when it is dense, each series
  from its own offset. `marker: true` puts one on every point.
- The legend shows each series' sign: its line with its marker, or a square.
- The theme's eight series colours were chosen for colour-blind readers (neighbours stay apart), and each stands at
  least 3:1 against the chart's background, in light and dark; text stands at 4.5:1. A test holds these contrasts.
- In forced colours (Windows high contrast), the chart takes the system's colours and keeps its symbols.

## Motion

A chart appears and changes with a short, sober animation. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` there is none: the
end state shows at once. `animation: false` turns it off for every reader.

> The chart does its part; the page does the rest: give the chart a title, put it near the text that speaks of it, and
> say in `description` what a reader should see in it.

---

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/theming-rtl/ -->

# Theme and right to left

A chart draws its shapes from the options and takes every colour and font from CSS variables. Its words, numbers and
dates follow the page's language, and its layout follows the page's direction.

## The theme sheet

`@dzgraph/theme/dzgraph.css` sets the variables, in a cascade layer named `dzgraph.theme`: any rule of your own that
is not in a layer wins over it, whatever its specificity. Load it once:

```ts
import '@dzgraph/theme/dzgraph.css';
```

`dzgraph.unlayered.css` is the same sheet without the layer, for an app whose own reset is not in a layer and would
otherwise win over the theme. Without either sheet a chart draws its geometry but no colours: no colour is written in
the library's code.

The variables come in two families: `--tz-*`, the palette shared with DzGrid and DzTooltip (a page that themes its
grids themes its charts), and `--dzgraph-*`, the chart's own.

| Variable | What it sets |
|---|---|
| `--tz-bg`, `--tz-fg`, `--tz-fg-muted`, `--tz-border`, `--tz-accent` | the shared palette: background, text, muted text, lines, accent |
| `--dzgraph-series-1` … `--dzgraph-series-8` | the series' colours, in a fixed order |
| `--dzgraph-background`, `--dzgraph-plot-background` | the chart's and the plot's background |
| `--dzgraph-text`, `--dzgraph-text-muted` | titles, labels, legend |
| `--dzgraph-axis-line`, `--dzgraph-tick`, `--dzgraph-grid-line` | axes, ticks and gridlines, kept quiet |
| `--dzgraph-focus` | the keyboard's focus ring, the zoom band |
| `--dzgraph-others`, `--dzgraph-track` | a pie's « Others » slice, a gauge's empty scale |
| `--dzgraph-font-title`, `-subtitle`, `-axis-title`, `-tick-label`, `-legend`, `-data-label` | the fonts, by role |

## Light and dark

Each colour of the theme is a light and dark pair (`light-dark()`): the chart follows the page's `color-scheme`. A
`data-theme="light"` or `data-theme="dark"` attribute on the chart or one of its parents chooses one; this site sets
it on the page, which is why its switch changes the charts too. A picture exported keeps the colours of the screen,
unless it asks for another theme (see [Export and print](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/exporting/)).

## Your colours and fonts

Set the variables on `.dzgraph`, the class of every chart, with the values of your own design system:

```css
.dzgraph {
  --tz-accent: var(--brand-accent);
  --dzgraph-series-1: var(--brand-primary);
  --dzgraph-color-harvest: var(--brand-harvest);
  --dzgraph-font-title: 600 18px var(--brand-font);
}
```

A series takes the palette's colours in order. `color: 3` gives it the third; `color: { token: 'harvest' }` gives it
`--dzgraph-color-harvest`, a variable you define. A colour is never written in the options, so a theme change reaches
every chart. Past eight series the palette starts again, and each series keeps its own marker symbol.

The eight colours of the palette were chosen together: neighbours stay apart for colour-blind readers, and each holds
3:1 against the background in both modes. When you replace them, check the same.

## The chart's words

The chart's language is the `locale` option when it is given, else the `lang` of the chart's element or its nearest
parent, else the browser's. It sets the numbers and dates (`Intl`) and the words: « No data », the summary and the
points' names for screen readers, the menu, the data table. English and French are built in; any other language
writes its numbers and dates in its own way, with English words, until you give yours with `messages`:

```ts
import { column } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart, type MessageOverrides } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const words: MessageOverrides = {
  noData: 'Nothing picked yet',
  seriesHidden: (name) => `${name} put away`,
  seriesShown: (name) => `${name} back`,
};

chart(
  document.getElementById('picked')!,
  { locale: 'en-GB', series: [{ type: 'column', id: 'picked', name: 'Picked', data: [] }] },
  { types: [column], messages: words },
);
```

The language and direction are read again at every drawing: a page that switches them sees its charts follow.

## Right to left

A chart takes the direction of its element (its `dir` attribute or its CSS `direction`), unless the options give
`dir: 'rtl'` or `'ltr'`. Right to left is designed in, not added:

- Everything placed by reading direction changes sides: the title starts on the right, the legend runs from the
  right, the y axis stands at the start (on the right) and an `opposite` one on the left.
- Bars grow from the start side, the right.
- The x axis is not mirrored: categories and time still run left to right, as is most common for numbers and dates.
  `mirror: true` runs them right to left, and the arrow keys turn with it.
- Numbers and dates are written by the locale: its digits, its separators and their order.
- A label in the other direction (a Latin name in an Arabic chart) keeps its own direction inside its box.

This chart's element is in Arabic, right to left; its title and series names stay in this page's language:

> Write CSS with logical sides (`inline-start`, `margin-inline-end`) around a chart too: the same page then reads well
> in both directions.

---

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/angular/ -->

# Angular in depth

`@dzgraph/angular` gives two standalone components: `<dz-chart>` and `<dz-sparkline>`. The
[Angular](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/getting-started/angular/) page draws a first chart. This page goes further: options made from signals,
what each output carries, the chart's methods, two charts that follow each other, sparklines, and the server.

## Inputs

| Input | What it is |
|---|---|
| `options` | Required. The chart's `ChartOptions`. A new value updates the chart. |
| `types` | The series types the chart may draw; else those of `provideDzGraph()`, else none. |
| `features` | The features the chart may use; else those of `provideDzGraph()`, else none. |
| `messages` | Words to use instead of the built-in ones. |
| `animate` | A hook to drive the animations yourself. |

`options` is compared by identity: give a new object, never change the one the chart has. A top-level field the new
value no longer has goes back to its default: take the title out, and the chart has none.

`types`, `features`, `messages` and `animate` are the chart's setup. A new value of one of them draws a new chart, and
the user's zoom, hidden series and selection start again. Keep them in fields of the component, as below.

## Options from signals

Make the options a `computed` of your signals. When a signal changes, the chart gets new options and updates. A
series that keeps its `id` is updated in place.

```ts
import { Component, computed, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { column, type ChartOptions } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { crosshair } from '@dzgraph/dom';
import { DzChart } from '@dzgraph/angular';

type Shop = 'harbour' | 'market';
const HONEY: Record<Shop, readonly number[]> = {
  harbour: [14, 22, 19, 27, 31, 26],
  market: [9, 12, 18, 24, 29, 35],
};

@Component({
  selector: 'app-honey',
  imports: [DzChart],
  template: `
    <button type="button" (click)="shop.set('harbour')">Harbour shop</button>
    <button type="button" (click)="shop.set('market')">Market stall</button>
    <dz-chart style="block-size: 320px" [options]="options()" [types]="types" [features]="features" />
  `,
})
export class Honey {
  readonly types = [column];
  readonly features = [crosshair];
  readonly shop = signal<Shop>('harbour');
  readonly options = computed<ChartOptions>(() => ({
    title: { text: 'Jars of honey sold (made up)' },
    crosshair: true,
    xAxis: { scale: 'category', categories: ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May', 'Jun'] },
    series: [{ type: 'column', id: 'jars', name: this.shop() === 'harbour' ? 'Harbour shop' : 'Market stall', data: HONEY[this.shop()] }],
  }));
}
```

## What each output carries

Each event of the chart is an output of the same name. Most outputs carry the event's detail, as `on()` gives it. A
few carry the useful part only:

| Output | `$event` |
|---|---|
| `pointHover` | the point under the pointer (`PointRef`), or null when it leaves |
| `pointClick`, `pointFocus` | the point (`PointRef`: `seriesId`, `index`, `key`) |
| `rangeChange` | the visible range (`min`, `max`), or null for the whole data |
| `modeChange` | the mode: `'zoom'`, `'selection'` or `'measure'` |
| `problems` | the list of problems |
| `legendToggle`, `viewChange`, `measure`, `selectionChange`, `drill` | the event's detail |

So `(pointClick)="open($event.seriesId, $event.index)"`, not `$event.point`.

## The chart's methods

The component's `chart` is the chart itself, with all its methods. It is null before the chart is drawn (after the
first render, in the browser) and on the server, so call it with `?.`.

The user's view (zoom, hidden series, selection, comparison) is plain data. Here a button keeps it, and another brings
it back:

```ts
import { Component, viewChild } from '@angular/core';
import { line, type ChartOptions, type ChartView } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { zoom } from '@dzgraph/dom';
import { DzChart } from '@dzgraph/angular';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-saved-view',
  imports: [DzChart],
  template: `
    <dz-chart style="block-size: 300px" [options]="options" [types]="types" [features]="features" />
    <button type="button" (click)="keep()">Keep this view</button>
    <button type="button" (click)="restore()">Back to the kept view</button>
  `,
})
export class SavedView {
  readonly dz = viewChild.required(DzChart);
  readonly types = [line];
  readonly features = [zoom];
  readonly options: ChartOptions = {
    title: { text: 'Bees seen per hour (made up)' },
    series: [{ type: 'line', id: 'bees', name: 'Bees', data: [12, 30, 52, 61, 58, 44, 23] }],
  };
  private kept: ChartView | null = null;

  keep(): void {
    this.kept = this.dz().chart?.getView() ?? null;
  }
  restore(): void {
    if (this.kept) this.dz().chart?.setView(this.kept);
  }
}
```

## Two charts that follow each other

`linkCharts()` from `@dzgraph/dom` links charts: the same crosshair, the same zoom, the same selection. In Angular,
link them once both are drawn. Each `<dz-chart>` draws its chart after the first render; a `read` callback of
`afterNextRender` runs after that, in the same render.

```ts
import { column, line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart, crosshair, linkCharts, zoom } from '@dzgraph/dom';

const heat = chart(
  document.getElementById('heat')!,
  { title: { text: 'Heat (made up)' }, crosshair: true, series: [{ type: 'line', id: 'heat', name: 'Heat (°C)', data: [14, 17, 21, 24, 23, 19, 15] }] },
  { types: [line], features: [crosshair, zoom] },
);
const bees = chart(
  document.getElementById('bees')!,
  { title: { text: 'Bees seen (made up)' }, crosshair: true, series: [{ type: 'column', id: 'bees', name: 'Bees', data: [12, 30, 52, 61, 58, 44, 23] }] },
  { types: [column], features: [crosshair, zoom] },
);
const unlink = linkCharts([heat, bees], { crosshair: true, zoom: 'x' });
```

A chart destroyed leaves its links by itself; `unlink` stops them all.

## Sparklines

`<dz-sparkline>` takes `values` (required; `null` is a gap) and `options`: `type` (`line`, `area`, `column`,
`winloss`), `min` and `max`, `markers` (`last`, `minmax`, `none`), `label`, `locale`, `messages`. A new value of either
draws it again. Its `sparkline` gives its `problems`.

Give several sparklines the same `min` and `max`, and they compare:

```ts
import { Component } from '@angular/core';
import { DzSparkline } from '@dzgraph/angular';

type Hive = { readonly name: string; readonly weights: readonly number[] };

@Component({
  selector: 'app-hives',
  imports: [DzSparkline],
  template: `
    @for (hive of hives; track hive.name) {
      <p class="hive">{{ hive.name }} <dz-sparkline [values]="hive.weights" [options]="{ type: 'column', min: 0, max: 40, label: hive.name }" /></p>
    }
  `,
})
export class Hives {
  readonly hives: readonly Hive[] = [
    { name: 'Hive A', weights: [12, 18, 25, 31, 36, 38] },
    { name: 'Hive B', weights: [10, 11, 15, 14, 19, 22] },
  ];
}
```

A sparkline is 6em by 1.2em, in line with the text. Size it with the app's global CSS, on `.dzgraph-sparkline` (the
drawing is made by script, so a component's scoped styles do not reach it):

```css
.hive .dzgraph-sparkline { inline-size: 8em; block-size: 2em; }
```

## On the server

On the server, both components draw nothing and fail on nothing; `chart` and `sparkline` stay null. The host
`<dz-chart>` is there, as a block: give it its height in CSS, and the page does not move when the chart arrives in the
browser.

> The components draw in the browser only, after the first render. Code that needs the chart runs there too: in an
> event handler, or in `afterNextRender`.

---

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/dztooltip/ -->

# DzTooltip

A chart has its own tooltip: a card beside the point under the pointer or the keyboard focus. With
`@dzgraph/dztooltip`, [DzTooltip](https://github.com/plinthworks/dztooltip) draws it instead, with its look: its
placements, tones, shapes and animations, the same as the other tooltips of your page.

The chart still decides what the tooltip says and when it shows. DzTooltip decides where it goes and how it looks.

## Install

```sh
npm install @dzgraph/dztooltip @dztooltip/core @dztooltip/theme
```

Load DzTooltip's theme once, beside DzGraph's: `@dztooltip/theme/dztooltip.css`. Only `@dzgraph/dztooltip` imports
`@dztooltip/core`: a chart without the bridge ships none of DzTooltip.

## Use it

`dzTooltip()` makes a feature: give it to the chart with the others.

```ts
import { line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart, crosshair } from '@dzgraph/dom';
import { dzTooltip } from '@dzgraph/dztooltip';

chart(
  document.getElementById('bees')!,
  {
    title: { text: 'Bees seen per hour (made up)' },
    crosshair: true,
    xAxis: { scale: 'category', categories: ['08:00', '10:00', '12:00', '14:00', '16:00', '18:00'] },
    series: [{ type: 'line', id: 'bees', name: 'Bees', data: [12, 30, 52, 61, 44, 23] }],
  },
  { types: [line], features: [crosshair, dzTooltip({ tone: 'info', placement: 'top', animation: 'morph' })] },
);
```

This site does not load DzTooltip, so the chart below shows the chart's own tooltip. With the bridge, the same words
show in a DzTooltip bubble.

## The look

`dzTooltip()` takes DzTooltip's look options. The main ones:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `placement` | Where the bubble opens beside the point: `top` (the default), `bottom`, `start`, `end`, with `-start` or `-end`, or `auto`. |
| `tone` | Its colours: `info`, `neutral`, `success`, `warning`, `danger`. |
| `animation` | How it opens and closes: `fade`, `scale`, `slide`, `pop`, `rise`, `morph`, `none`. |
| `shape` | A ready-made shape of `@dztooltip/theme`, or your own as SVG path data. |
| `flip`, `shift` | Whether it moves to the other side, or slides along, to stay in the window. |
| `maxWidth`, `offset` | Its widest, and its gap from the point. |
| `reducedMotion` | Under reduced motion: no animation (`none`, the default) or a short fade (`fade`). |

The bridge adds two of its own: `nonce`, the page's nonce for the one `<style>` DzTooltip adds under a strict CSP, and
`root`, the element the bubble goes in. DzTooltip's [documentation](https://github.com/plinthworks/dztooltip) has the
rest.

## What stays the chart's

- **The words.** The heading, a row per series with its sign, name and value, the shares and totals: the chart's, in
  the chart's language and direction.
- **When.** Shown at once on the point under the pointer or the focus, moved from point to point, hidden when the
  pointer leaves the plot, on Escape, and on a tap outside. DzTooltip's hover delays do not apply.
- **Screen readers.** The bubble is for the eyes only. The focused point's name and the chart's live region say the
  same, as without the bridge.

> As every DzTooltip tooltip, a scroll of the page hides it. The next point pointed at or focused shows it again.

---

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/guides/dzgrid/ -->

# DzGrid

`@dzgraph/dzgrid` puts a chart beside a [DzGrid](https://github.com/plinthworks/dzgrid) grid, in two ways:

- `linkGrid()` links a chart and a grid that show the same rows: what the user selects on one side is selected on the
  other.
- `chartFromGrid()` fills a chart with what the user selects in the grid: a block of cells, rows ticked, or the pivot.

The bridge reads the grid through the parts it uses, without importing DzGrid: any DzGrid 1.x fits.

## Install

```sh
npm install @dzgraph/dzgrid
```

## A point is a row

A point and a row match by key: a point's `key` is its row's id, the one DzGrid's `getRowId` gives. Give each point
the key of its row, and the link finds it. A key one side does not have is skipped, never an error.

## Link a chart and a grid

`linkGrid()` links them and returns the function that unlinks. By default the selection goes both ways: the points
the user selects in the chart become the grid's selected rows, and the rows ticked in the grid become the chart's
selected points. Neither echoes back. The chart needs its `selection` feature and option.

```ts
import { column } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart, selection } from '@dzgraph/dom';
import { linkGrid } from '@dzgraph/dzgrid';
import { createGrid } from '@dzgrid/dom';
import { EN } from '@dzgrid/dom/locales/en';

type Hive = { readonly id: string; readonly hive: string; readonly honey: number };
const HIVES: readonly Hive[] = [
  { id: 'h1', hive: 'Hive A', honey: 14 },
  { id: 'h2', hive: 'Hive B', honey: 22 },
  { id: 'h3', hive: 'Hive C', honey: 9 },
  { id: 'h4', hive: 'Hive D', honey: 17 },
];

const c = chart(
  document.getElementById('honey')!,
  {
    title: { text: 'Honey by hive (made up)' },
    selection: true,
    xAxis: { scale: 'category', categories: HIVES.map((h) => h.hive) },
    series: [{ type: 'column', id: 'honey', name: 'Honey (kg)', data: HIVES.map((h) => ({ x: h.hive, y: h.honey, key: h.id })) }],
  },
  { types: [column], features: [selection] },
);
const grid = createGrid<Hive>(document.getElementById('hives')!, {
  rows: HIVES,
  getRowId: (h) => h.id,
  messages: EN,
  columns: [{ id: 'hive', header: 'Hive' }, { id: 'honey', header: 'Honey (kg)', type: 'number' }],
  selection: { mode: 'multi' },
});
const unlink = linkGrid(c, grid);
```

`selection: false` turns the selection off. A grid's « every row but these » selection (select all, over server
pages) is not carried to the chart: the chart cannot know rows it was never given.

## Filter the grid by the chart

With `filter`, the link sets the filter of one column of the grid. The user's filters on the other columns still
apply.

| `filter` | The grid shows |
|---|---|
| `{ column, by: 'selection' }` | the rows whose `column` holds the key of a selected point; none selected, no filter |
| `{ column, by: 'range' }` | the rows whose `column` number is in the chart's visible range; the whole data, no filter |
| `{ column, by: 'range', as: 'instant' }` | the same, for a date-time column |

For a range, the filter is set once a zoom or a pan rests, not at every frame: a grid fed by a server asks once.
While linked, the link owns that column's filter. Unlinking lifts it, unless the user has set another since.

## A chart from what the grid selects

`chartFromGrid()` fills a chart the app made: its element, its features, its title stay yours. The bridge gives it
its `series` and its `xAxis`. The data comes from the first of these that applies:

1. the grid's **pivot**, when it is on (`pivot` given): its groups as categories, one series per created column;
2. a **block of cells** (`range` given, two cells at least): its rows, its columns;
3. **rows ticked**: those rows, in the grid's order, every visible column.

With none of them, the chart keeps what it shows: a click outside the grid drops its block, and the chart must not
empty when the user moves to it.

```ts
import { column, line } from '@dzgraph/core';
import { chart } from '@dzgraph/dom';
import { chartFromGrid } from '@dzgraph/dzgrid';
import { createGrid } from '@dzgrid/dom';
import { EN } from '@dzgrid/dom/locales/en';
import { EN_RANGE } from '@dzgrid/dom/locales/en-range';
import { range } from '@dzgrid/dom/range';

type Month = { readonly id: string; readonly month: string; readonly apples: number; readonly pears: number };

const blocks = range();
const grid = createGrid<Month>(document.getElementById('fruit')!, {
  rows: [
    { id: 'jan', month: 'Jan', apples: 5, pears: 1 },
    { id: 'feb', month: 'Feb', apples: 8, pears: 2 },
    { id: 'mar', month: 'Mar', apples: 6, pears: 3 },
  ],
  getRowId: (m) => m.id,
  messages: { ...EN, text: { ...EN.text, ...EN_RANGE.text } },
  columns: [
    { id: 'month', header: 'Month' },
    { id: 'apples', header: 'Apples', type: 'number' },
    { id: 'pears', header: 'Pears', type: 'number' },
  ],
  selection: { mode: 'multi' },
  features: [blocks],
});
const c = chart(document.getElementById('fruit-chart')!, { title: { text: 'Fruit picked (made up)' }, series: [] }, { types: [column, line] });
const stop = chartFromGrid(c, grid, { range: blocks });
```

The user selects the block from Jan to Mar, Month to Pears. The chart shows this:

## How columns become series

- **The points' names.** Among the columns before the first number column, the first text, choice, yes/no, day or
  date-time column names the points. A date-time column puts them on a time axis, in the grid's zone (`timeZone`,
  UTC by default); a day column too, at their midnight. Any other puts them on a category axis, with the text the grid
  shows. With no such column, the points are evenly spaced.
- **The series.** Each number column is a series, named by its header, its id `grid:` and the column's id. Other
  columns are left out.
- **The values** are what the grid shows, its edits included, never its formatting. A blank, or a value the column
  refuses, is a gap. A point's key is its row's id, so `linkGrid()` finds it.
- **The type.** `type` if given; else a line on a time axis, and columns otherwise. The user's choice in the chart's
  menu wins.

By default the chart follows: it is filled again when the user changes the block or the rows ticked, and when the rows,
the columns or the pivot change — once a frame at most. `follow: false` takes one picture. Rows ticked by code do not
refill it, so `linkGrid()` beside it does not shrink the chart to its selection.

`gridTable()` gives the same table without a chart: its `source` (`pivot`, `block`, `rows` or null), its `xAxis` and
its `series`.

## A menu item

`chartMenuItem()` makes an item for DzGrid's cell menu. It calls your function with the cell's context; the label is
yours, in your app's language.

```ts
import { chartMenuItem } from '@dzgraph/dzgrid';
import { contextMenu } from '@dzgrid/dom/context-menu';

type Month = { readonly id: string; readonly month: string; readonly apples: number };
declare function openChart(month: string): void;

const menu = contextMenu<Month>({
  items: (_cell, defaults) => [...defaults, chartMenuItem('Chart', (cell) => openChart(cell.row.month))],
});
```

Put `menu` in the grid's features, beside the `range` feature.

> The values and the labels reach the chart only: its tooltip, its table, its exports. Never a problem, never an event.

---

<!-- https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/options/ -->

# Options

One page per option, in six groups. Each page starts with the option's facts, read from the library's sources, then
says what it does, with an example and often a live chart.

## The groups

| Group | What it holds | For instance |
|---|---|---|
| Chart | the top-level keys of `ChartOptions` | [`title`](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/options/chart/title/), [`aspectRatio`](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/options/chart/aspect-ratio/) |
| Series | the keys every series has, whatever its type | [`data`](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/options/series/data/), [`id`](https://plinthworks.github.io/dzgraph/options/series/id/) |
